title: Dental Answering Service: Costs, Coverage & AI Options
summary: What a dental answering service costs, how after-hours dental calls are handled, and where the calls you miss actually end up, with federal ED data.
body_markdown:
A dental answering service picks up the calls your practice cannot: after hours, at weekends, during a procedure, or when the front desk is already on another line. An operator answers in your practice's name, handles routine requests, and escalates genuine emergencies to the on-call dentist.


The case for one is usually made in terms of patient satisfaction. The more concrete argument is what happens when nobody answers: **nearly two million Americans a year present at an emergency department with a non-traumatic dental problem** : a toothache, an abscess, an infection. The ED can manage the pain. It cannot treat the tooth.


This guide covers what dental answering services cost, how after-hours dental calls should be handled, and how the traditional model compares with the AI systems now entering the category.


## Key Takeaways


-


**1.93 million treat-and-release ED visits for non-traumatic dental conditions in 2019** , costing $469.9 million in hospital costs. These are overwhelmingly problems a dental practice could have managed.


-


**Dental emergencies need their own escalation criteria.** Avulsed teeth are genuinely time-critical; facial swelling can be dangerous; most toothaches can wait until morning. A generic "urgent or not" script does not capture that.


-


**Published rates run about 1.30–1.43 per minute** for traditional answering services. AI alternatives run lower and can book directly into the schedule.


-


**New-patient calls are the commercial argument.** Dentistry runs on new patients and hygiene recall. A missed new-patient call usually goes to whoever answers next.

Median cost of a treat-and-release visit in 2020 for patients aged 64 and under was **158**fornon-traumaticdentalconditionsand**292** for traumatic. The 2020 fall reflects pandemic-year emergency department avoidance rather than any improvement in access.


The non-traumatic figure is the one that matters for a dental practice. These are not accidents. They are toothaches, abscesses and infections, conditions that are painful enough to drive someone to hospital at 11pm, and that a dentist treats routinely. An emergency department will typically manage symptoms and refer the patient back to a dentist, which means the clinical problem is unresolved and the patient has paid for a visit that did not fix it.


Not all of those visits are preventable by a practice answering its phone, and many involve patients with no regular dentist at all. But a meaningful share begins the same way: someone in pain calls their dental office, nobody picks up, and the ED is the only other door that is open.


## What a dental answering service actually does


The standard capability set, consistent across providers:


-


**24/7/365 live answering** in your practice's name


-


**Appointment booking, confirmation and rescheduling** , though usually captured as a request rather than written into your system


-


**New patient intake.** Capturing details and insurance information


-


**Emergency triage and escalation** to the on-call dentist under criteria you define


-


**Prescription refill requests** routed for authorisation


-


**Bilingual support** , commonly English and Spanish


Providers split into three groups. **Generalist answering bureaus** with a dental landing page: AnswerConnect, Posh, Ansafone, Answer California, MAP Communications. **Dental-native platforms** such as[Weave](https://www.getweave.com/dental-phone-answering-service/) , which positions its phone answering as built into the practice communication system rather than outsourced. And[AI entrants](https://www.sully.ai/blog/ai-medical-receptionist) including Dapta and Whippy, which answer and increasingly book directly.


The question that separates them is the same one that separates medical answering services: does the call come back to you as a message, or as a booked appointment?


## Dental emergencies need dental escalation criteria


This is where a generic answering service script fails a dental practice, and it is worth writing your own rules rather than accepting a template.


Dental urgency does not map onto a simple urgent/not-urgent split. Three broad tiers are useful:


**Time-critical, page immediately.** An avulsed permanent tooth is the clearest example: reimplantation outcomes depend on minutes, and the caller needs instruction before they arrive. Facial swelling, particularly where it affects the eye, the floor of the mouth or breathing, warrants immediate escalation and may warrant directing the patient to an emergency department.


**Urgent, same day or next morning.** Uncontrolled bleeding after an extraction, a fractured tooth with exposed pulp, a lost crown on a prepared tooth, severe pain unmanaged by over-the-counter analgesia.


**Routine, morning message.** Most toothaches, a lost filling without pain, a chipped tooth, sensitivity, routine scheduling.


An operator cannot make these determinations clinically; they are not licensed clinicians, and should not improvise. What they can do is apply your criteria accurately, which is only possible if your criteria are written down and specific. "Use judgement" is not a protocol.


Two things to specify explicitly:


-


**What the caller should be told to do** in each tier, including the avulsed-tooth instruction, which is time-sensitive and standard.


-


**Who gets paged, how, and what happens if they do not answer** , meaning the failover chain, not just the first number. The same[on-call routing design](https://www.sully.ai/blog/after-hours-medical-answering-service) applies in medical practices.


## New patient calls: the commercial case


Dentistry is unusual among healthcare settings in how directly new-patient calls convert to revenue, and how substitutable practices are to a caller.


Someone with a toothache calling at 6pm is not loyal to your practice. They are calling a list. If you do not answer, the next practice does, and that patient is now in someone else's recall system for years.


This is the argument that justifies coverage independently of the clinical case. It also changes what good looks like: for a new-patient call, taking a message is weak, because the patient is still unbooked and still calling other practices. Booking them into an actual slot while they are on the phone is the outcome worth paying for, and it is what[Sully.ai's AI Receptionist](https://www.sully.ai/agents/receptionist) is designed to do, and it is the main thing the AI systems in this category do that the traditional ones do not.

Whichever you choose, pin down the same details: the billing increment, whether hold time is billable, setup fees, holiday and bilingual surcharges, and the overage rate.

The practical test: count how many after-hours calls last month were genuine emergencies versus scheduling. Most practices find the split is heavily administrative, which argues for handling the majority automatically and reserving human escalation for the minority that needs it.


## HIPAA applies here too


A dental answering service hearing a patient's name and reason for calling is handling PHI, which makes it a business associate.[HHS requires](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html) satisfactory assurances in a signed business associate agreement before PHI is disclosed, the same standard that applies to any medical vendor, and it applies to AI providers and human services identically.


Ask: will you sign a BAA covering every service we enable; where are your operators located; how are messages containing PHI transmitted; how long are recordings retained; and for AI vendors, which subcontractors process call audio and do you hold BAAs with each.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### How much does a dental answering service charge?


Published rates run about 1.28–1.43 per minute. MAP Communications lists $49/month pay-as-you-go through $649/month for 500 included minutes. AI alternatives built for healthcare publish 0.75–1.00 per minute. Most dental-specific providers do not publish rates and quote after a consultation.


### How much does a medical answering service cost?


The same range applies, because these are usually the same providers with a different landing page. Expect $1.30 per minute as a reasonable benchmark for live human answering, with the real figure driven by billing increment, overage rate and surcharges rather than the headline price.


### Is there a free dental answering service?


No. Any service handling patient calls is handling PHI, must sign a BAA and maintain safeguards, and that carries cost. Voicemail is the free option, and it is the one that produces the emergency department outcome described above.


### Can an answering service book appointments into our practice software?


Some can read and write to your schedule; many only capture a request for your team to action in the morning. For new-patient calls this distinction is the whole value, because an unbooked caller is still ringing other practices. Confirm it specifically before signing.


### What counts as a dental emergency after hours?


Clinically time-critical cases include an avulsed permanent tooth, uncontrolled bleeding, and facial swelling affecting the eye, floor of the mouth or breathing. Severe unmanaged pain and fractures with pulp exposure are usually urgent but not immediate. Most other calls can wait until morning. Write your own criteria rather than accepting a generic script: the operator applies your rules, not clinical judgement.


### Should dental practices use AI or a human answering service?


Split by call type. Scheduling, rescheduling, new-patient intake and routine questions are handled well and more cheaply by AI, which can also book directly. Genuine clinical emergencies should reach a person under clearly defined criteria. Most practices benefit from both rather than choosing one.


### Will an answering service reduce emergency department visits for our patients?


No provider can promise that, and you should be sceptical of any that does. What the federal data establishes is that roughly 1.9 million non-traumatic dental ED visits occur annually and that these are largely conditions dentists treat. Whether answering your phone changes any individual patient's decision is not something the evidence can tell you.
